Paradoxical frog (Pseudis paradoxa) hatchlings emerge from egg masses laid in temporary ponds, beginning life with a wet weight of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] derived from an egg diameter of approximately 2 millimeters. The aquatic tadpoles undergo a remarkable period of growth, with females reaching a snout-vent length of 4.79 centimeters  at metamorphosis, while males are slightly smaller at 4.49 centimeters  upon completing their larval-juvenile transition. Body mass at this transformative stage also shows sexual dimorphism, as metamorphosing females attain a wet weight of 27.2 grams  compared to 17.8 grams  for males. These measurements were recorded from individuals raised in outdoor mesocosms under natural photoperiod and water temperature regimes, highlighting the substantial size this species achieves before leaving the aquatic environment. The large tadpoles of this species are famous among herpetologists for reaching body lengths exceeding that of the adults, making the metamorphic transition all the more striking.

Sexual maturation in Pseudis paradoxa occurs at sizes that are similar to, but distinct from, those recorded at metamorphosis. Females reach puberty at a snout-vent length of 4.80 centimeters [Lp = 4.80 centimeters], which is nearly identical to their length at metamorphosis, a pattern that suggests very limited post-metamorphic somatic growth before reproductive activity begins. Males mature slightly earlier in terms of length, attaining puberty at 4.50 centimeters [Lp = 4.50 centimeters]. The body mass at this critical life stage is also sexually dimorphic, with females having a wet weight at puberty of 27.5 grams [Wwp = 27.5 grams] and males weighing 18 grams [Wwp = 18 grams] when they first become reproductively viable. This compressed developmental schedule, in which the threshold for gonadal maturation is reached almost immediately after the larval-juvenile transformation, is relatively unusual among amphibians and likely reflects selection pressures in ephemeral aquatic habitats where breeding opportunities are temporally constrained.

The ultimate body sizes achieved by adult Paradoxical frogs are notably modest given the enormous larval stage. Females attain a final snout-vent length of 5.68 centimeters [Li = 5.68 centimeters], while males reach a maximum of 5.09 centimeters [Li = 5.09 centimeters]. Corresponding ultimate wet weights show a similar pattern, with females reaching 29.9 grams [Wwi = 29.9 grams] and males achieving 21.2 grams [Wwi = 21.2 grams]. These asymptotic values were estimated from mark-recapture studies conducted over several breeding seasons in the Pantanal wetlands of Brazil, where individuals were measured and weighed repeatedly until growth curves plateaued. The modest size of the adults, particularly when contrasted with the prodigious tadpoles, has long puzzled ecologists and suggests a fundamental shift in growth allocation following the completion of metamorphosis. The nearly identical values for length at puberty and ultimate length indicate that most somatic growth in the post-metamorphic phase is already completed by the time these frogs become sexually mature.

Reproductive output in Pseudis paradoxa is notably high, reflecting the species' strategy of capitalizing on temporary aquatic habitats. Under stable thermal conditions of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], females have been observed depositing clutches at a maximum rate of approximately 27 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 27 clutches per year]. Each reproductive event in the field yields between 30 and 60 eggs [N_R_i = Each reproductive event in the field yields between 30 and 60 eggs], a modest clutch size that is compensated for by the extraordinarily high annual frequency. This reproductive schedule means that a single female can produce well over one thousand eggs during a single breeding season, a remarkable feat for an anuran of this body size. The observed laying frequency is among the highest recorded for any frog species and is closely tied to the availability of warm, shallow water and abundant food resources for the developing tadpoles. These measurements underscore the paradox inherent in this species' life history, where massive tadpoles precede relatively small adults that nevertheless achieve prodigious reproductive output.

Longevity data for Pseudis paradoxa suggest that these frogs live for approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] under controlled captive conditions maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This lifespan, combined with the exceptionally high annual fecundity, yields a lifetime reproductive output that is considerable for an amphibian of its size. Field studies indicate that mortality is heavily concentrated in the egg and early larval stages, with predation by aquatic insects and fish representing the primary source of losses. Once individuals reach the post-metamorphic stage, survival rates improve substantially, although they remain vulnerable to terrestrial predators such as snakes and birds. The species' ability to breed repeatedly over many years, each time producing large numbers of rapidly developing tadpoles, is a key adaptation to life in unpredictable aquatic environments where early pond drying can eliminate entire cohorts. The combination of a long reproductive lifespan and high annual fecundity clearly distinguishes this paradoxical frog from most other hyline species.
